utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We regret that Judge Nosworthy is not with us this morning for urgent personal reasons. We do expect that she will join us later in the day, and we have in these circumstances decided that it is in the interests of justice to continue in her absence meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination will continue in a moment, but please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence yesterday will continue to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let me remind you where we broke off yesterday. We were talking about meetings of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff, first the one held on the 23rd of October when General Perisic explained that the group that was in Podujevo would withdraw since there were no activities there, but at the same time he retained the right to return that group. Then you described to us how the negotiations went and what General Perisic said at the negotiations to Generals Clark and Naumann and what their response was. After that we talked about the collegium of the 26th of October, a day after the negotiations, when General Dimitrijevic practically confirmed what General Perisic had said; that is to say that he retained the right to return the troops if the KLA continued its attacks. And we moved on to December, also in relation to what had happened in Podujevo. Yesterday we also went through a very frank discussion between Generals Perisic and Ojdanic when General Ojdanic opposed the keeping of any kind of combat troops in the area. You also told us yesterday about the documents that you had, that the General Staff had, on the basis of the reports received from the liaison team with the OSCE mission and we started discussing the collegium of the 25th of December -- sorry the collegium of the 30th of December, 1999, where there was a discussion about these events. From the discussion one can see that General Dimitrijevic had the opposite view, and he said that the unit was withdrawn so that the KLA would be provoked. Could you please give me your comments as to what General Ojdanic's response was, or rather, what his opinion was and what his information was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit P928, the English version page 17, paragraph 1. The B/C/S text page 18, the last three paragraphs. Could you scroll it down a bit, please. [In English] No, no, sorry, previous page in the B/C/S, I believe, page 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, towards the bottom of the page you have what General Ojdanic said. Could you give us your comments on these remarks as you understood them.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I already spoke about this problem related to Podujevo and the assertion or opinion presented by General Dimitrijevic on the basis of the overall situation that it can be assumed that that unit left allegedly in order to provoke in the area where it went. I don't think that's right because General Ojdanic in his remarks at the collegium, he presented his view that perhaps the marching route that was selected was not a good one, the one that that unit had taken. However, if we look at the essence of the task that that unit had, we may conclude that this has to do with realisation of regular training of soldiers who had joined that unit at those training grounds. Any other conclusion in relation to the stay of that unit in that area at that point in time would be unacceptable, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you had confirmation from several sources for this assertion. One was the report that you received through the liaison team, and I see here that General Ojdanic is speaking about a conversation with the army commander. Who was commander of the 3rd Army at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be pointed out here that the Chief of General Staff, or rather, General Ojdanic then had contacts with the army commander, who roughly said that to him. And then the commander of the 3rd Army was General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General Ojdanic quotes General Perisic [sic] here. Does that correspond to what General Perisic indeed told the NATO representatives at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, is that the correct English page we have?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: No, it is not the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On English it should be page 17, paragraph 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is page 17 --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It must begin over the previous page. The matter is on the screen, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only General Ojdanic's name is on the previous page, but his remarks start on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in this text General Perisic quotes General Ojdanic. Is that what you heard General Ojdanic saying to the representatives of NATO during the negotiations on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is reliable information. At the talks that I attended with General Clark that General Perisic had, indeed, said that if the agreement is abided by, fine; if the agreement is not abided by, if the other side abuses it, then he retains the right for himself to return troops to the area. This was confirmed in these talks, and he accepted this; namely, that if they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, as I understand it you're being asked your recollection of what General Ojdanic said, not your recollection of what General Perisic said. Am I misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I think that we have a problem with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That was exactly what Mr. Visnjic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this text General Ojdanic quotes General Perisic and you can see that in the English text --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you look at page 4, line 22, you say: "In this text General Perisic quotes General Ojdanic" --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's mistake in my mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's General Ojdanic quoting General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move on can you clarify one thing for me, is the point -- one of the points being made here that General Ojdanic supported the withdrawal of all the units not just the one in the Podujevo area but the other three as well or is all of this evidence about the unit operating exclusively in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, during the talks, at the time of the negotiations, that is, in October, General Ojdanic supported the position that all troops should be withdrawn to barracks. Now in December we are only talking about the problem pertaining to this unit that has to do with Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's reassuring because that's how I had understood it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let me be precise once again. General Perisic in this text quotes General Ojdanic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll have to repeat this yet again. General, in this text General Ojdanic quotes General Perisic. Does this correspond to what you heard General Perisic saying to representatives of NATO during the negotiations in Belgrade on the 25th of October in 1998. You can give us a brief answer. We've received enough information about this.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right, Mr. Visnjic, because I am so familiar with this subject matter as I was a participant in these talks. General Perisic told General Clark what I had already presented; namely, that if the other side does not honour the agreement he would retain the right for him to return part of the units to the area and that pertained to the unit that had to do with Podujevo, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, once again may I remind you in the report of the liaison team from the 24th of December that was shown to you yesterday, that is to say the liaison team of the 3rd Army, what is stated is that the representatives of the mission had been informed - I think that that is the date, the 24th of December - that this unit would remain in the area longer nevertheless. In these remarks made by General Ojdanic what is stated are the reasons for that. General, was this roughly correspond to what was discussed at the collegium and to your own recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received reports from the liaison team of the 3rd Army, in which information was provided to the effect that the mission had been notified of the fact that this unit went out to the training grounds. The mission was following that. In the talks that General Ojdanic had with General Dimitrijevic, he was not opposed to training at all; however, he did express some dissatisfaction of his as to whether the moment was right, whether that was the right point in time. So from our side all the commitments stipulated in the agreement had been met.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We are going to move on to our next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is Racak. Could we please prepare P939. In English it is page 31, the last paragraph, and page 32, first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is the collegium held on the 21st of January, 1999, held a few days after what had happened in the village of Racak. At this collegium you discussed these events, am I not right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that meeting of the collegium there was a discussion on the report that we received from the subordinate command in relation to the situation that had occurred on the 15th of January concerning the village of Racak. The Chief of General Staff asked, since from various sides there was information coming in as to what was going on in the village of Racak, and the position of the army in that. There was a discussion in order to reach the full truth. The Chief of General Staff ordered his deputy, General Marjanovic, that he should lead the group that would, on the basis of information received from subordinate commands, from diplomatic representatives and others come to the truth, the complete truth because General Ojdanic insisted that the full truth be established as to what happened in Racak and what they position of the army was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether this is P939. It should be the collegium of the 21st of January. I've just been informed that the date is wrong on this date, the 24th of December, but it is the document that I'm looking for. So could we please have a look at the first page. Your Honour, I think that it is clear now. Nevertheless, this is the document dated the 21st of January, 1999. It is obvious, however, that at the bottom of the page it is the 24th of December that is typed out. But I think I can proceed now that we've dealt with that. I do apologise. Could the witness please be shown page 31, the last paragraph, and the first and second paragraphs on page 32 and the corresponding pages in English, or rather, B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a problem, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think I have a problem. Maybe I'll go on on another -- [Interpretation] Perhaps I'll move on to the next exhibit and come back to this one later because I seem to have a problem with this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, we'll come back to this one later because we're having technical problems at the moment, so we'll come back to this exhibit later on. But now let's go back to the cooperation of the Army of Yugoslavia with the verification mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 3D409, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the Chief of the General Staff designated you. What was your function in relation to cooperation with the mission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the collegium of the General Staff, there was a discussion when the agreement was signed and when we received from the federal government the obligations taken on by the state in relation to the missions. It was said that at the level of the General Staff a group, a team, should be formed of senior officers to implement this task. The Chief of the General Staff ordered that I be the leader of that team, and the team also included representatives of almost all the sectors and administrations of the General Staff. Two assistants were designated, General Panic was my deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 2 in English, paragraph 3, please, that's point 5 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this order signed by General Perisic it was established how you were to report to the Chief of the General Staff. Could you please tell us what this actually looked like. How did you most often inform the Chief of the General Staff about your work and contacts with the verification mission.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was authorised on behalf of the Chief of the General Staff to attend sessions of the Federal Commission which were held as a rule once a week. Secondly, I received daily reports from the liaison team from the 3rd Army, and the chief -- and I usually reported to the Chief of the General Staff at the collegium concerning the conclusions and problems discussed at the Federal Commission. If there were any urgent issues arriving on a daily basis, I would go and see the Chief of the General Staff personally to inform him. However, mostly information was given at the collegium so that all the members would be informed about all the problems concerning our tasks and the mission in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, if we look at all the collegium sessions in that period of time, we can get a more or less complete picture about the relations of the Army of Yugoslavia with the mission and about what you reported to the General Staff and the Chief of the General Staff. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This was a new task, so to say, set before the General Staff and it was taken very seriously. That's why such a strong team was formed including the commanders of the armies, where teams were also set up, headed by generals leading those teams mostly in the 2nd and 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D405, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move off this. In that paragraph 5 it says there will be daily reports with regard to the OSCE and NATO missions. What was the NATO mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a mission -- well, agreements were signed with the OSCE and NATO regarding the anti-aircraft defence in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There wasn't a separate mission of people from NATO present on Yugoslav territory, though, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were our representatives. Three officers who were designated in Vincenza, and when it was concluded that a security air zone should be established, all the anti-aircraft defences were withdrawn from Kosovo and they monitored this. This had to do with the NATO mission in Kosovo and Metohija. NATO representatives were located, as far as I know, within the command of the air force in Zemun at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we will have a witness here who will say more about this NATO mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, 3D405, that's the Defence exhibit we're looking at. This is a document entitled: "Overview of the obligations and tasks and the methodology of work stemming from the agreement with the OSCE mission on the verification mission in Kosovo." This is a very broad title. Can you tell us what the tasks of the Army of Yugoslavia were or, to be brief, are the tasks of the Army of Yugoslavia contained in the document we see before us now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document drawn up by the federal government, the state was behind it, and almost all state institutions were given obligations concerning the verification mission in Kosovo, and this includes the army. If you look at this overview, the army was given significant tasks connected to the missions starting from receiving accommodating, providing health care, coordination, assistance, and all the other tasks linked to setting up the OSCE and NATO mission in Kosovo. Based on these tasks set by the top leadership of the state, in the General Staff it was said that the army should, in a planned and organised manner, carry out all these tasks in compliance with orders from the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The document speaks for itself. We will go into it in detail later on, but let's move now to 3D411, instructions concerning the relations of the Army of Yugoslavia and the mission. General, when was this document drawn up?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the obligations taken by the army and the General Staff, the General Staff ordered the team to draw up certain documents which were necessary for this mechanism to function, the mechanism of relations between the army and the OSCE and NATO mission. And this document was one of these. It was compiled right after the agreement was signed in October 1998, in late October.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The army, in fact, prepared a booklet containing a set of documents concerning the implementation of the agreement; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We compiled a study in the General Staff, and that was the liaison team for liaison with the missions, and it was delivered to all the subordinate commands, the 2nd and the 3rd Army. And in conversations with General Clark, General Perisic showed him that document and he presented to him a copy of the first edition on that evening when we had the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. General, I would like now to comment on page 4, paragraph 2 of these instructions. Yes, yes, here we see paragraph 2. I'm especially interested in this last sentence, what does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, in the General Staff it was estimated that this was a new task for the army as a whole because I have to say that apart from the team that was designated, all the organs of the General Staff were duty-bound in their areas of responsibility to contribute to implementing our relations with the mission as successfully as possible. The Chief of the General Staff concluded that this was one of the more difficult tasks before the General Staff in the forthcoming period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And that's what it says in paragraph 4 of this same document; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This was the conclusion reached at the collegium. The General Staff set up not only a team, but also all other organs were included and each one had to carry out tasks relating to the functioning of our relations with the missions in Kosovo within their area of competence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, I didn't understand the answer about the last sentence in paragraph 2. The answer didn't seem to relate to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let's take another look at the last sentence in paragraph 2. What does this refer to? How was this situation envisaged, the situation in which the army was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as it's defined here, all the commands, units, and institutions of the army shall base their relations with the OSCE and NATO verification mission until Kosovo and Metohija on respect to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the FRY, however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not what you're being asked, you're asking about the last sentence which is in English in a different form of script, the part about armed attacks on members.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to answer that. If it should happen that in our communications there is activity by the terrorist forces - I'm referring to armed attacks on individuals or units or facilities of the army - the army would respond according to the rules of combat of use of units. This refers to the terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand, but why do you have that in this document? What's the purpose of putting that sentence in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The purpose was to link this up with the previous one because relations are based on respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the FRY, and this was threatened in a manner of speaking by terrorism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But did you have reason to think that your units would act outwith the rules of combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Our units, as a rule, always acted according to the rules of combat then in force in the Army of Yugoslavia. It says here, "armed attacks shall be repelled according to the rules of combat."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it just -- I have to say it seems to me an odd sentence in the context of the document itself. But please continue, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, if I may put an additional question in relation to this sentence. Does this perhaps refer to a situation where no special approval is needed to repulse an attack?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in peacetime commanders were duty-bound to take certain measures to oppose various forms of terrorism so that no special order was required.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, let's see how reporting is regulated in this document. The B/C/S, or rather, the English text at page 5, last paragraph, and in B/C/S it's page 6, first paragraph, or rather, second paragraph. General, how at the time when General Perisic was Chief of the General Staff, how was reporting regulated?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean reporting on the work of the missions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Contacts with the missions and reporting, or rather, informing the missions on the activities of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were duty-bound through our representatives in all the units to establish almost daily contacts with the members of the mission in Kosovo, and this was done. In this particular case - this has to do with the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps - we had teams in those commands and we had liaison officers in the subordinated commands. And in the course of the day, feedback was given as to what kind of contacts had been established and the General Staff received this feedback, both in the operative daily reports and in the reports sent by the teams from the 3rd Army. And there was discussion on particular issues at the weekly sessions of the Federal Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you have now before you page 6 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we also have page 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, it says here that the teams and liaison officers are to submit weekly reports; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was envisaged in the agreement. Reports were to be submitted as to the movements of units or company level or above in Kosovo, and those who arrived in Kosovo from the interior and in Kosovo itself as well as incidents in which units of the army participated and the measures taken by the members of the army who participated in the incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll ask you something now about the movements of the units in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P925, please. That's a record from the collegium meeting of the 27th of November, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, that's the day you had a meeting with General Andreja -- Drewienkiewicz. At that meeting you reported, or rather, you briefed General Ojdanic at the collegium and this was his first working day, in fact, about the current relations with the verification mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown in the English text page 14, paragraphs 2 and forward -- 2 to 10, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is your contribution to the discussion. You are briefing those present on several points, but what I wish to draw your attention to is the paragraph in English at the bottom which begins with: Lastly, General: "We draft these monthly reports and they insist on being informed in advance of our movements ..." What does this refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the responsibility to submit reports on what would come next, for the next session, what happened at this one. However, within the framework of these conclusions there were a number of different problems because this was the modus operandi. The report could have been abused with the focus on the opposite side. Because if the activities for the army for the next day were presented, this sort of information could be misused, leaving the army in a position of inferiority, which might then be taken advantage of by the terrorist forces, and they would probably be the ones to abuse this sort of information and take some sort of action based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What was your greatest concern, what sort of situation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was sort of present. According to some assessments, requests were made that were not provided for in the agreement, that access should be granted to certain facilities, especially problematic was the request about the members of the mission exercising control inside barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show B/C/S 14, page 14; English page 16, paragraph 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Here is your contribution and here are the reservations you express, and General Ojdanic had something to say, didn't he? Can you tell us what.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 6 in both B/C/S and English. [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Ojdanic insisted that there was information that the army was bringing in fresh forces, and General Ojdanic insisted that we should not be concealing anything but that we should have the right information and that we should give the members of the mission complete information, which is what they were to be familiarised with. And this is exactly what was done. He ordered me, or rather, the sector for this to function, among other things, because the mission kept on growing that we, too, should adjust to this newly arisen situation, that we should spot certain drawbacks, and I'm sure there were drawbacks in our work, too, so that we might be able to carry out our task as successfully as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. At the end of this collegium --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. It may be the translation, but you said General Ojdanic insisted that there was information that the army was bringing in fresh forces and insisted we should not be concealing anything. Now, what is the reference to bringing in fresh forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was information that was present. However, as far as we were concerned, this was nothing that we didn't -- was presented to the members of the mission. At the time, no fresh forces were being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But your sentence -- your paragraph -- or your answer, rather, began that: "He insisted that there was information that the army was bringing in fresh forces ..." Now, was -- were fresh forces being brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there was no information. There was information -- no fresh forces were being brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, are you saying that between October and March there was no change in the representation of the VJ in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was change in December when the new generation of soldiers came in. That was when one generation left the regular military service and a new generation came in, and then there was a change among the soldiers throughout the army, including the units of the Pristina Corps. Now, this was a special activity, this was planned, and this sort of information was made available in full to the members of the mission, the mission in its entirety. That's what one means by fresh forces. These were no fresh forces. This was just a new generation of soldiers being drafted and an old generation leaving the ranks of the army. Young soldiers were coming in, were being trained, and this was used to bring up the manpower levels of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you say that these rotations or movements were reported to the KVM in advance of them happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this information was announced when there would be the rotation of the soldiers and the numerical strength that will be conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Over the period from October until March, was there any increase in the representation of VJ forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to what I have stated, that there was a planned rotation of some soldiers already in March, when the situation assessment was such that there might soon be a NATO intervention, some of the units were brought to the edge of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was done sometime in March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there no occasion when a rotation of forces was taking place that the forces who should have left Kosovo nevertheless remained there so that the bringing in of their replacements actually increased the number of forces there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those soldiers who were being replaced, they went -- they went home. And in March, by a decision of the relevant state authorities, the regular military stint was extended for some soldiers in March 1999, for a group of soldiers, because of the situation which was such that an assessment was made, that there would soon be an intervention by NATO from the air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So those soldiers were held back and they remained in their units, not just in the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps, but rather throughout the VJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you please go to page 17 of the B/C/S, paragraphs 5, 6, and 7. In English the reference is page 19, paragraph 6 and 7, and page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand counsel. Can he please repeat the reference for the page and paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is about a conclusion by General Ojdanic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. English text, page 19, paragraphs 6 and 7, and page 20, paragraph 1, 2 and 3. Page 19 Dragoljub Ojdanic -- no, I think it's previous page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you have before you the contribution of General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please just show the Serbian text, next page, top of the of the next page, English. [In English] Next page in -- yes, that's okay. I'm sorry, English page was okay. English page, let's go back to page 19. And B/C/S page 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: There, General, you have General Ojdanic's contribution before you now. As for the second paragraph, it reads: "I personally believe that exceptional efforts and hard work are in store for us not least when the entire verification mission arrives." Please, in the light of what was discussed at the meeting, comment. I'm talking about the prep meeting for meeting with General Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is when the extent of the mission grew to considerable extent. The overall situation was analysed as well as the army's responsibilities. There was pressure for us to respond in an adequate manner to the situation we were now facing. General Ojdanic said that there would be a lot of hard work in store for us and a lot of effort, especially after the mission got there. This was a large-scale mission, and it needed insight into everything that was going on in Kosovo on an everyday basis, and we had to respond to this challenge from the level of the General Staff down to the lowest-ranking bodies. In March we started an analysis, throughout which we reorganized our functioning in relation to the mission, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown 3D438.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, these are minutes from the meeting with General Drewienkiewicz. You were at that meeting, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there when General Ojdanic talked to General Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: As you were being proofed for your testimony, you went through these notes. Is it consistent with how you remember the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I looked at it and this is the gist of what their conversation focused on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let me draw your attention to one thing, page 2 in the Serbian, there's a problem about protocol which was to be drawn up between the mission and the VJ. In English this is page 3, paragraph 4. General, can you tell me who General Pellnas was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a representative of the OSCE. He was the representative of the OSCE in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what about General Drewienkiewicz, he was also an OSCE man, but he was their representative in the verification mission, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know- and I think I'm sure- he was Walker's deputy in Kosovo and Walker was the heads of mission in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a look at this. General Pellnas is here suggesting that a protocol should be drawn up and signed to avoid any possible limitations and problems in the VJ's cooperation with the mission. On the other hand, in this same document on page 3 of the Serbian, which is also page 4 in, I think, the English. General Drewienkiewicz, on the other hand, or rather, I'm sorry it was on the same page. He says that six weeks had gone by already, time was running out, and he had no intention of wasting any time drawing up the protocol. In actual fact, OSCE people also had different positions as far as this was concerned, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was, in a way, a new kind of relationship and various methods were tried in terms of carrying out the task. So the Chief of the General Staff ordered that a protocol, set of instructions, be drawn up as to how the methodology would be applied in relation to the verification. We drew up these instructions and we offered this set of instructions to the mission in Kosovo and Metohija; however, General Drewienkiewicz did not accept our protocol instructions in their entirety. He believed he needed no such instructions. He had the agreement, he had the provisions of the agreement, and he thought that in a way he could do as he saw fit because he had the powers to carry out any task that was entrusted to him. So the protocol was not accepted in its entirety by the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Could you please look at 3D557. This is the collegium held on the 3rd of December, 1998. That is to say that after the meeting with General Drewienkiewicz you submitted to the OSCE mission the documentation that was required about arms, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inter alia full information was required that did exist in the General Staff. It had been done a lot earlier in accordance with Article 4 of the Vienna Agreement, subregional arms control, it was done by the department subregional arms control. It had to do with all the weapons from 82-millimetre calibre up, also combat vehicles, APCs, including air force attack, helicopters, and aircraft. This task was carried out and there were inspections coming from other states and our inspection teams went to other states in order to act in accordance with the provisions of the Vienna Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We'll deal with that later. Can you look at page 6, paragraph 2 of the English text, and could you explain to us, this is yet again some remarks by General Ojdanic. What kind of a letter is this? You and General Panic are being ordered here to study a letter that has to do with the verification mission, the OSCE verification mission. What kind of a letter is this? What was the position of General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the collegium we were made aware by the Chief of General Staff that a letter had been sent by General Walker --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Sorry, General --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Page 6, paragraph 2 -- I'm sorry, B/C/S page 5, paragraph 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, General. You see here General Ojdanic's remarks, and there's a reference to you and General Panic as persons who are supposed to study a letter to the president. What was this letter and what is it that you and General Panic were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a few moments ago that at the collegium General Ojdanic said that some letter had arrived to the president of the republic from the head of the mission, Mr. Walker and a task was given. When the content of this letter is received as well as the political positions of the top echelons of the state that we should study this carefully and see what it is that is required in that letter by the head of the mission, what the obligations were of the army based on that letter, and that he would do his best to try to get this letter from various institutions, if necessary, even from the president himself, that is what he said at the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D786.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did General Ojdanic set up a Working Group from the General Staff that was supposed to tour the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps and see what the situation was in respect of cooperation with the OSCE mission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We analysed the overall situation, we followed the situation and with a view to rendering assistance to the subordinate -- well, I say "subordinate" conditionally. It all did not go that way. If I'm speaking of the chain of command there was this expert team from the General Staff and these officers were basically on the team, these officers who were the most familiar with the subject matter related to missions and they were sent to the area of the 3rd Army, basically to Kosovo in order to carry out a control, render assistance to this team and to the liaison officers so that they would function as well as possible, that is to say this mechanism, so that problems would be noticed, so they would be mutually resolved and in the forthcoming period this task would be carried out as successfully as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, just one thing can we explain something to the Trial Chamber. If you say "conditionally subordinate," tell me, the mission, the liaison team of the 3rd Army, it was not subordinate to the liaison team of the General Staff; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not a chain of command. This was an organisation. Everything went through the Chief of General Staff. The Chief of General Staff was the only one who could issue orders. So this was -- this was an organisation within the function of command that carried out this task. And naturally, I contacted the Chief of General Staff and he regulated this through his orders and this was also done by the subordinate commands through their orders in terms of engagement of parts related to the mission in the army and the corps because I was directly subordinated to the Chief of General Staff with regard to this particular issue, I was related to him in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the leader of the liaison team of the 3rd Army, he was directly subordinated to the commander of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and in the Pristina Corps to the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down, note the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, you referred to a letter from Walker to the president. Did you actually see the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally did not see this letter. I just received instructions from the Chief of General Staff that pertained to the army that were contained in this letter, this letter that had sent by Mr. Walker to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the plan had been that you and Panic should see the letter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were supposed to study the provisions of that, that which related to the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean study the provisions of the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the positions that were presented there that the Chief of General Staff conveyed to us. He told us to study this well and, in a way, analyse what pertained to the army and the functioning of the army vis-a-vis the missions in that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the position was relayed to you without you ever seeing the letter? That's all I want to be clear about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me -- let's move on to 3D787.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This Working Group toured the units, the units of the 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps, and when it returned it submitted a report. General, you are aware of the content of that report; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As we can see in this document, the Working Group submitted a report to the leader of the team in the General Staff; that is to say, the team for liaising with the OSCE and NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. This report deals with problems in great detail. I would like us to have a look at this in greater detail, too. I would like to ask you for your comments regarding paragraph 2 on this same page, it starts with the following words: "The mission of the OSCE on several occasions..." Et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is presented here is that the members of the mission have been trying to verify that which pertains to the Vienna Agreement, or rather, we thought that was not necessary. Then some information is presented here that were allegedly present regarding the lack of cooperativeness on the part of the army, and also that some positions were not defined in relation to the provisions of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a more precise question, General. There was an order of the Chief of General Staff, General Perisic, dated the 16th of November, 1998, whereby the representatives of the mission were forbidden from entering barracks; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The point was that they insisted that they enter the barracks, too, that they tour the premises, that they talk to individual soldiers to count the personnel, I'm saying this conditionally, and the weapons and so on. We thought that was not regulated by the agreement and that that was impermissible before a political decision was made that this could not be done without an order of the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, problems are referred to with regard to verification of certain incidents in the field.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement defined that members of the mission have the obligation to control cease-fires and to verify incidents that took place in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. However, the task was that once this verification was over to create joint minutes that would be signed by both sides. I don't know why, but some missions sometimes did not want to sign these minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 of this document. Your Honours, if you look at paragraph 5 in the English, it's still in front of you, it says: "The following positions of the commission of the government of the FRY are explained ..." And then we move on to the next page. Can we move to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And, General, would you look at paragraph 5 of this document. Not to be into great detail. Paragraph 5 itself is self-explanatory. Just tell me, were these the positions that the army was duty-bound to carry out in view of it function in the implementation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are positions that were presented by this expert group and this is contained in the report and these are the positions that the army was carrying out. As you can see what is allowed is verification of activities, entry into barracks is not allowed, and one of the conclusions was to control and monitor cease-fires. As far as I know, there weren't any combat activities in barracks, and therefore it was not necessary to monitor cease-fires in places where they were not taking place, like the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We are going to move on to our next document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask what may seem a naive question, but perhaps you can assist me. Pretty fundamental to the agreements that were reached in October was the level of forces, the numbers of forces, within Kosovo. How did you envisage that being verified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A plan was made in the General Staff about transporting that group of soldiers that was supposed to go to Kosovo to replace the units. This transportation took place by rail mostly. A plan was made as to when this group, so to speak, would arrive at the railway station in Kosovo, and the exact number of soldiers was notified; that is to say, these new soldiers that were supposed to come in, the new generation, that was fully submitted to the verifiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you expected them simply to take your word for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's not for taking our word for it. Full information was provided by this, exact personnel levels of the soldiers arriving in the territory of Kosovo for replacing the generation that was supposed to withdraw from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you any idea what would have -- what was the difficulty about allowing inspection of barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the agreement did not envisage that because the Vienna agreement implied control, arms control, of 12.7-millimetre calibres, larger calibres, so what was left was counting personnel levels and light weaponry, and there was relatively little of that, given the peacetime formations, and there was no political decision made to carry out verification of what was in the barracks without a special order of the Chief of General Staff in relation to such activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So there was no problem? There was nothing you could see, apart from the terms of the agreement, lay that aside for a moment. There was no problem for you about barracks being inspected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had that been agreed, there would have been no problem whatsoever to have that carried out, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to dwell on this document for a few more minutes because at the end of this document -- I'll just go through the English text. Towards the bottom of page 2 there is a heading that says "proposals." Then can we move on to page 3 in the English, and at the same time I would like to ask that the Serbian text be moved to page 3 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you see these proposals well, the proposals made by the commission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now, in view of the question that was put to you by the Judge and in view of what we had discussed, can we go through the proposals one by one and can we hear from you what was done with regard to every one of them. Was a protocol and verification made by the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the order of the Chief of General Staff, a protocol was made and it's part of the document that can be seen that was submitted to all units and I said a few moments ago well, this was also given to General Clark so what was done was--

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just slow down. This needs to be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for the methodology of relations between members of the army and the verification mission, in order for it to be defined in detail as to what should be done together --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you know whether a new protocol was done in December, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the situation -- the newly created situation that necessitated the updating of these documents, we did update them every now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's move to point 2 of these proposals. The positions of the federal government, are they built into the order issued by the General Staff in relation to the missions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was presented by the federal government was discussed, and everything that pertained to the army was built into the documents drawn up in the General Staff, and in the tasks of the army in relation to the missions from the highest to the lowest levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 3, minefields --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, though, is the one that's relevant to the issue of barracks inspection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Obradovic, is this something that you undertook following this document? You were the president of the liaison committee, were you -- commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the team leader in the General Staff for relations with the missions, and I acted for the Chief of the General Staff in the Federal Commission. He was a member of that commission, but I went to the meetings on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you'll see in this paragraph 2 that there was a request to be made to the commission to forward positions on the verification of VJ forces, equipment, and unit activities in written form. Was that done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said that at the Federal Commission. I presented the request of the General Staff that positions linked to monitoring of the barracks should be put in writing. This referred to monitoring the units in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We expected these positions to be delivered to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And were they put in writing? Were you given authority to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received the political position that until it is politically defined, monitoring of units in the barracks is not to be allowed until further notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Whose decision was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was a decision of the federal organs, the decision of the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you help me more specifically? Who would be in a position to make that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what the president of the Federal Commission told me, Mr. Sainovic, he told me this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to draw your attention to the last sentence which says: "The positions are to be incorporated in the VJ and GS order," and this order will be our next document so Your Honour will be able to draw conclusions from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move to point 3, marking of minefields. I don't know how relevant it is to this case. Point 4: "Consider the possibility of correction on the extended border area on the 3rd Army team of experts' proposal." General, briefly, if you are familiar with this team of experts, was this done? What was done in relation to the border area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that at that time they were working on it and that the border area was extended because circumstances required it. I was aware of that. As you can see, the team of experts in a way concluded that this would be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Point 5, just a brief comment, why was a special administration requested?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a time when we already had quite a bit of experience. We noticed certain weaknesses and omissions on our part. This was something new for all of us who were working on it, and as this was a voluminous task, a very large task, at the collegium of the General Staff they wanted to avoid any significant failures or omissions in future work, in future dealings with the mission. The mission had increased in size on all the areas on Kosovo and Metohija; that's why we thought that a separate administration should be set up in the General Staff dealing only with this job and that it should be a sort of organisational entity in the General Staff dealing with relations with the missions and which could go into these matters in depth, down to the last liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And point 6: "Consider the proposed organisational structure of the VJ liaison teams and officers" refers to the same problem. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of our conclusions, that the structure that had existed up to that point - and we already had a new organisational structure of the teams in depth - that this should be analysed once again and that in accordance with the newly arisen situation the number of officers should be increased, especially officers, liaison officers, for the missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I assume that point 7 refers to the same activities in proving the organisation of the work?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Chief of the General Staff said quite a few times that apart from this, many other officers from the General Staff, starting from the generals, should have a place in these activities and these teams so that the tasks can be carried out as best possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, point 8, that's an important paragraph because I see that the proposal here is to carry out daily exchange of information with the mission, the OSCE mission, that is, as opposed to the weekly exchange of information which had occurred previously. Let me remind you that in the document we saw yesterday, which is a report of the liaison team of the 3rd Army of the 25th of December, that the liaison team of the 3rd Army was presenting a certain position, that is, that daily reporting to the OSCE mission would be burdensome for them. But the General Staff Working Group in spite of this proposed that there be a daily exchange of information.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the opinion of the Working Group was justified because there were quite a few activities going on, and for the system to function in the best possible way information should be exchanged on a daily basis, although that had already been done but that this should be made official and that exchange of information between representatives of the mission and the liaison officers in Kosovo and Metohija should take place daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And points 9 and 10, these have to do with technical improvements, including motor vehicles, mobile telephones, recruiting interpreters, and so on and so forth. General, these proposals of the Working Group headed by Colonel Kosta Novakovic, were they accepted by you and by the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a complex discussion where the Chief of the General Staff ordered all sectors, for example, equipping with motor vehicles, that would belong to the rear; and then recruiting additional liaison officers, that would be a task for the personnel and mobilisation sector; and then officers had to be found in other units and other parts of the army who could speak English and that their language competence should be checked so that we could fulfil our tasks in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 3D408 page 1. We will be looking at pages 1 and 2. This is an order of the Chief of the General Staff of the 23rd of December, 1998, 23rd of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is one of the documents in which the proposals of the Working Group were implemented; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see, in the heading it says: "In accordance with the demonstrated need, experience is gained so far in working with the missions. This now should be all brought together, and therefore the Chief of the General Staff ordered that a single protocol for verification of activities of the VJ be drawn up and that the representatives of the army who were in the team," and then it mentions General Mladenovic and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the conclusions of the federal government commission are mentioned here. Is that the document that General Ojdanic requested from you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The newly arisen situation required a response to this question, and therefore this followed in accordance with the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document was commented on by General Loncar, so I do not wish to go through the same material again, but it provides the information the General has testified about today. This is a summary document containing everything that has been said so far. Could we now see P939. This is the collegium of the 21st of January, 1999. In English it's page 33, paragraph 5. Your Honours, I definitely seem to be having a problem with this document so I'll move on and I'll sort it out during the break. 934, the 11th of February, 1999, the collegium of the General Staff, P934, please, page 20 in English and 19 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I'll ask you the following. You attended these meetings of the Federal Commission. At any of these meetings was a conclusion made that the army had been uncooperative?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the methodology of work at the Federal Commission, analyses were made by sector of the total situation, and it was concluded that there were no elements indicating that the army had been uncooperative up to that point on any significant issue. As a whole, it was concluded that the army had carried out its tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And also in this discussion which is several pages long, pages 20 to 22 in English, let's not go into details now, the reasons for the reorganization of the team are enumerated here. I'm asking you this because there's more than one theory as to why the liaison team was reorganized. Could you tell us briefly, what were the reasons for reorganizing the liaison teams in the beginning of 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've just said, the overall situation was being monitored, as was the implementation of the given task. As the mission increased and grew in numbers, more of our officers were required to be in present in places where verification was carried out. So we concluded that we had to increase the number of liaison officers and that we also had to include -- increase --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- The number of officers who spoke English, that interpreters should be increased in number and that these officers should be released from their other duties which they had been carrying out according to the establishment because this was a very delicate matter, working with the unit and also appearing in contacts with members of the mission who had daily requests for contacts. So these were the substantive reasons why based on information coming from below and the assessment of the General Staff that the situation had to be revised in order for things to function as best -- in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see P941 of the 25th of February, 1999, page 23 in English, paragraphs 4, 5, and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you were aware that cooperation was not ideal, that there were certain problems in cooperation with the OSCE. Did you discuss this at meetings of the collegium? Was there any discussion of errors committed by our side in the course of ...

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, needless to say, whenever a task is received it must be analysed both in terms of its positives and its negatives, and I must try to be objective here, specially at the outset despite the enormous efforts that we were making in the General Staff and especially officers down the chain of command because in addition to liaison officers some other officers from both the brigades and the battalions had to be involved in contacting the mission. Entire mechanism had to be kept busy with this task in order for it to be carried out in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we pull up the page up to the very top, the English page, and can we please go to the next page where there's something about General Obradovic. Can we go to the next page, please, 22, in English, the last paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your last question hasn't been answered, but perhaps you can seeking the answer somewhere else on the document. Your last question was: "Was there any discussion of errors committed by our side?" And it doesn't seem that there were any errors. Maybe that's the answer you expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, were there talks at the collegium about any mistakes made by our side and were there attempts, rather, was an analysis made of our own mistakes?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to say that we analysed the overall situation, and we noticed certain mistakes which were understandable, especially at a tactical level over there, in a bid to respond to all the requests made by the verification mission. There were mistakes. Obviously, these were then analysed by the General Staff, and the Chief of the General Staff was adamant that we should get at the truth of what exactly was going on, how this was working, and that measures would be taken in a timely manner to help those people so that they would be able to carry out their own tasks. This was frequently discussed at the collegium of the General Staff to keep the number of mistakes down, to give direct assistance to the officers who were in contact with the mission, and to avoid any misunderstanding wherever possible to keep them down to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure if this is a good time for our morning break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you have only a question or two on this document you should complete it, bearing in mind the technological problems we can have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just going to show the witness something, but it's not appearing on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what is it you want to see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to see is his contribution. Maybe we can get that and he can comment. I can see the Serbian now down towards the bottom of the screen. [In English] Yes, that's okay. And English version should be paragraph -- yes. Also -- [Interpretation] pull the English page all the way down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you look at the paragraph that begins with the following words, or rather, with the word: "Next."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. There was discussion about this at the collegium and I said that we should not be in a situation where we concluded that we were not able to analyse our own mistakes at each level in relation to the mission. I pulled no punches here. I said that one needed to review the situation so that we might be able to give timely assistance and to make good any mistakes that were made and keep mistakes down to a minimum. This was one of the conclusions that were reached and there was permanent pressure by the Chief of the General Staff and all the other members of the collegium to the effect that we should pay close attention to all the reports to see what our responsibilities were at the level of the General Staff and to provide assistance down the chain of command to keep the whole thing working as smoothly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I look at this last sentence of this paragraph, General, you requested daily reports on omissions and mistakes of both parties, our party and the verification mission, too?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was adamant that this should be done. I was one of the most responsible people as far as this particular job was concerned. I asked the Chief of the General Staff in no uncertain terms that he should send out an order down the chain of command for written reports on violations to be submitted on exceeding one's authority, and also everything that had to do with any actions taken by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think this would be a good time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Obradovic, we have to break at this stage for half an hour, and would you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we shall see you again at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Can we -- can we show the witness Defence Exhibit P935. This is the 11th of March collegium, the 11th of March, 1999, page 11, paragraph 4, paragraph 5, and paragraph 6. [In English] English version. Page 10, paragraphs 1, 2, and 3. Your Honours, what you see before you is the English version. The previous page contains the name of General Obradovic and nothing more. I would like to focus precisely on the three paragraphs that begin with the word "third." First, second, and third paragraph on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you spoke about reporting. You spoke about what you demanded from the teams to report on our mistakes and on the mission's mistakes, too. Can you comment on this contribution, this is the 11th of March, 1999, the collegium. This is about ten days before the war began.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, let me say this, the overall situation was analysed that prevailed in Kosovo and Metohija. We considered whether there was anything that could be done additionally to improve the implementation of our tasks. That's why this was discussed and a decision was later taken to send in some officers from some new units to improve our operations and to avoid any mistakes in communicating and working together with the mission that was in Kosovo at the time. This is what the situation required because the overall situation was growing in complexity, both domestically and abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say the overall situation was gaining complexity, both domestically and abroad, midway through the third paragraph there is a reference to the new focus on the border with Macedonia or on the border with Albania. Who pursued these activities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, the situation was getting more and more complex at every level and nothing was left to chance within the framework of this overall situation. Predictions were made as to what might happen over the short term in terms of combat-readiness, the general situation in the army, and in terms of the implementation of all our tasks and missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So what did you believe, General, at the time right follow over the short term in relation to the Macedonian and Albanian borders?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on assessments made by the General Staff which were in turn based on reliable information, the conclusion could be reached that there might soon be an act of aggression and that the border was under threat, very much so, in fact, especially from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. Could you now please, or rather, let us dwell on this for a minute longer. Despite this, improvements are being planned for your cooperation with the mission, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We believed at the time that efforts to avoid aggression would prevail and that we might be able to complete our tasks with the missions. That's why we reinforced our teams and sent some of the officers from some other units in order to be able to implement this task in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'll now be showing you two exhibits about efforts to cooperate with the Kosovo Verification Mission, the first one being 3D407. General, briefly what is this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see this document was produced early in March 1999. In addition to everything that had been done up to that point, the General Staff ordered that documents be studied such as the agreements mentioned here on the NATO and OSCE verification mission in Kosovo, that the resolution -- Security Council Resolution 1199 should be studied and all the resolutions that had been adopted earlier, and that based on this all measures should be taken so that any of our commitments and responsibilities might be implemented in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
