utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document runs into about four pages in Serbian, but despite that could we please show the last page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us about the diagram you can see in the Serbian, what is that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, this is one of the attachments to the study and this shows the organisational chart of organs that were appointed in the army to work with the OSCE and NATO missions. As you can see, there was a liaison team in the General Staff and they were in touch with teams in the 2nd and 3rd Armies and the air force, and then down the chain of command, as you can see. Down in Pristina there was a liaison team from the 3rd Army, a liaison team of the Pristina Corps, all the way down to liaison officers in garrisons wherever the units were, the VJ units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show the witness 3D784.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Please comment briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document contains conclusions that were reached earlier on at the collegium as to what was to be done in order for the system that had been set up in the army to function smoothly. Among other things, there was this order by the Chief of the General Staff to send some officers from some of the other units to detach certain officers that had other responsibilities and commitments under the establishment, and these officers were now sent to Kosovo. There was a three- or four-day seminar in Pristina that was organised where a team of experts from the General Staff organised to teach this seminar. Some members of the mission were there, and one of the talks was given by Mr. Drewienkiewicz who was the deputy head of mission. We tried to keep the contacts close between the mission and us on the one hand, the general objective being the completion of the mission's tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This document marks the end of our dwelling on the efforts made by the VJ in a bid to improve and enhance cooperation with the mission. General, you informed the collegium on several occasions about activities undertaken by the mission, the Kosovo Verification Mission, and the NATO mission in Kosovo. First of all, could you tell us what your sources were as far as the activities of these missions were concerned; and secondly, what were the salient features of the work of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information we got was just regular information, but we received through daily operative reports submitted to the command. I said that those who were working with the missions, each of their commands had a particular assignment. More accurate information was provided by the liaison team in the 3rd Army, in the Pristina Corps. Information was obtained based on analyses conducted by the Federal Commission. They had weekly discussions, among other things, about the work of the mission and there were other sources of information on the overall effect of the mission's work in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what were the salient features of their work, the work of the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the agreement, the focus of their work was to be an maintaining cease-fires, on monitoring movements by units, and on verifying any violations or clashes that were breaking out. However, in addition to this and despite all of their best efforts, there were elements that exceeded their purview and there were attempts being made by them to do things that were outside the agreement, at least the way we understood it. Additional information was sought, special problem was posed by their unannounced arrivals, their liaison officers, and them visiting the units unannounced, and this caused a great deal of hardship to the members of the mission but also to us because all these visits were unannounced and we had to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The 10th of December, 1998, collegium, and this is Defence Exhibit 3D484. English text pages 12 through 14. You and General Dimitrijevic spoke about the problem of notifications regarding replacements of groups of soldiers who were supposed to come to Kosovo, and I think that both you and General Dimitrijevic expressed certain reservations, reservations conveyed to you by the commander of the 3rd Army at that regarding notification concerning the time of arrival of the train with the recruits. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a planned activity that went from the level of the General Staff to the immediate personnel on the ground. It was a sizeable group, three and a half thousand soldiers I believe. I think this is reliable information. These were unarmed soldiers and they went only with some of the indispensable equipment carried by soldiers when they are being reassigned to another duty, and we were expressing our fear that perhaps they would be a target for the terrorists to ambush them. In that case, we would sustain losses without any possibility of reacting. That was quite justified, and I think in a way members of the mission were asked, although they received information as to when this train was supposed to arrive with that group of soldiers, and to protect them, to provide security, so that from that area they could go to different garrisons. They arrive in a single place and then they're supposed to be sent out to other garrisons and other units located in Kosovo and Metohija. So there was a fear of abuse by the terrorists and that there was the possibility of having these soldiers attacked, and these were just young soldiers who had just completed their initial training. And this fear was expressed by the commander of the 3rd Army, too. It was indispensable for the mission to protect them so that this task could fully be carried out in a safe way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now that you're talking about safety and security of this group of soldiers that arrived in December, what about the collegium of the General Staff, were they concerned about the safety of the verification mission, too, because according to the agreement one of the tasks of the army was to ensure the safety of the verification mission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We concluded, or rather, in accordance with the agreement and the positions presented by the federal government inter alia we established what the obligations of other institutions were, that is to say the MUP, for providing security for the verification mission. And if there is any kind of a special situation, the army should assist the MUP, I mean in these activities vis-a-vis the verification mission. If necessary, the army could be involved, too, this was one of our tasks because it was the state that guaranteed the safety and the security of the verification mission as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the English text page 15, last paragraph, of this same document, 3D484. These are the remarks of General Ojdanic. General Ojdanic -- well, let's wait for the B/C/S version but I'm going to read something out to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It's B/C/S page 16 paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the text appears I'm going to read it out. General Ojdanic says: "I put the question as to who was responsible in this country and who should ensure that what the FRY has signed too is carried out, that is to say guaranteeing the full security of the verifiers, and I was told that it was the MUP." And then he says: "In the event that the MUP forces could not carry this out, then the army should be involved too." General, that was the understanding of the army in terms of the security of the verification mission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a conclusion that was there, and I think it was quite clear to us who were engaged in that work, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're still on the same document can we look at page 16, paragraph 5 of the English, and B/C/S page 17, paragraph 2. It's the paragraph that starts with: "We have major problems ... In relation to a single interpretation of existing documents. This is the first attempt being made at federal level to resolve that. I said as far as the army is concerned it's an operative organisation and whatever is jointly concluded and delegated to us we can implement as quickly as possible, but it is not up to us to interpret the agreement reached."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, that was the position of General Ojdanic, and I assume that that fits into what it was that you stated before other state organs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole that was the position of the General Staff because the Chief of the General Staff insisted on everybody knowing what they were supposed to be doing, what the obligations of the other institutions were, so that we in the General Staff and the army know roughly what our obligations were and what our powers were. According to what you said just now, I never had any dilemmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at Defence Exhibit 3D558, collegium of the 6th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, within this month, we looked at the previous collegium meeting from the beginning of December and now we've moved on to the beginning of January. Something changed in respect to the verification mission, didn't it? In your view, what would be the characteristics of the activities of the verification mission in that period?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We analysed all these activities that were taking place primarily in the area of Kosovo and Metohija. In one analysis presented by General Dimitrijevic it was stated that the verification mission is acting in a one-sided manner. They focus on the army and on the MUP and there is no information regarding their attitude towards the other side. Secondly, it was our assessment that there were quite a few cases in which the verification mission overstepped its authority stipulated in the agreement. Thirdly, that this overall attitude implied that something was being done that was not indispensable if we look at the agreement, or rather, the documents that regulated the relationship of the army, or rather, the conduct of the army and of the mission in Kosovo. Information was provided there that the verification mission and the staff that is involved were predominantly ethnic Albanians; then they had frequent contacts with the members, or rather, those teams, staffs, of the terrorist forces. In some report it was stated that as a matter of fact members of the verification mission are submitting information to the other side about the activities of the army and movements of the army. So there was a danger of them deviating from their basic purpose and them dealing with some questions and tasks that were not defined in the agreement. This analysis, or rather, on the basis of this analysis it was possible to conclude that nevertheless in terms of certain elements members of the mission were deviating from the basic obligations they had according to the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: At the same time was there reinforcement of KLA activity, were they stepped-up and what was the effect of the mission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the beginning of January. In addition to all of this they were supposed to influence the other side so that terrorist activities not be carried out. As far as I can remember, in that period members of the army, soldiers, were abducted in the area of Bajgora. That means that this was a confirmed fact that the activities of the terrorists were particularly geared towards the army in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I will take the liberty of reading this text, page 10 in the English around the third paragraph, I'll read one of your conclusions that says: "There are some conclusions that terrorism that is being carried out now is basically aimed against the civilian population of both ethnic backgrounds and vis-a-vis the MUP. In the forthcoming period it is expected that it may be displayed against the members of the Army of Yugoslavia." You said that, General, on the 6th of January, 1999, at the collegium meeting. When were the soldiers abducted?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this confirms our assessment --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When, when, do you remember when the soldiers were abducted?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers were abducted on the 8th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. So that confirms that your assessment was --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conclusion that was presented at the collegium of the 6th of January, well on the basis of this reliable information was carried out and this fear was proven straight away to be a well-founded one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. P936, could that be prepared, please, the collegium of the 14th of January, 1999, the remarks of General Dimitrijevic, the English text page 10 paragraph 4. And the footnote, footnote 1, so that means that it's down there in the footnote. And these are the remarks of General Dimitrijevic. In the Serbian it is page 9. I think that you'll find your way. This is what General Dimitrijevic said and the footnote is probably from the document submitted by General Dimitrijevic. This footnote 1 says: "Part of the Albanian population believes that the verifiers are following every step made by the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP, preventing them to fire at the KLA, and they are submitting information about the MUP and the Army of Yugoslavia." And then certain examples are referred to. General, does this correspond to the information that General Dimitrijevic had otherwise also been sending to the General Staff concerning the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I say straight away that General Dimitrijevic was head of the security administration, I mean a man who very, very carefully monitored the situation and assessed it accordingly. The information he presented at the collegium and this specifically was information that really caused concern and this was presented at the collegium of the Chief of General Staff because that was what the actual state of affairs was, the conclusion that the civilian population believed some elements of the mission that they were following the activities of the army, that it was being made possible for them to supply them with weapons, basic necessities, food, and so on; this is a conclusion that led to a belief not that they had gone beyond the obligations stipulated in the agreement, but that conditionally speaking they had sided up with the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, I can't find this on page 10. Can you help me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just opened my copy. It is page 9. So could we look at the preceding page in English. English text. [In English] Down, footnotes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, what was done about these concerns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conclusion in accordance with what the head of the security administration was saying was to take measures through federal authorities, to try to have the verification mission ensure what was stated in the agreement, to prevent these terrorist activities as much as possible of the terrorist organisations in Kosovo and to make it possible to carry through those obligations stemming from the agreement related to cease-fires, especially to prevent an increase in terrorism in the entire area because you have seen for yourselves that in that period of time what happened was what I had stated earlier on, abduction of soldiers and stepping up terrorist activities in the broader area of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that's the conclusion. What I want to know is: What was actually done about these concerns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When this conclusion was put forward before the members of the collegium of the General Staff, certain measures were taken to ensure combat readiness to prevent the terrorist actions against the army, other institutions, and the population in Kosovo and Metohija. And the highest state organs were certainly informed of the situation in Kosovo in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that all that was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In March the situation was quite complex, as I've already said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is the 14th of January, isn't it? Why did nobody take this up with the -- why did no one take this up with the KVM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In contacts with the members of the mission, this was certainly discussed. General Loncar and the team leaders there discussed all of this in Kosovo and Metohija almost on a daily basis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, what you're claiming here is that there was discussion about KVM members operating in a one-sided manner, overstepping their authority, giving highly sensitive information to the KLA terrorists, and there was no formal protest, no letter written in this bureaucratic system that you have to Mr. Walker to raise the matter with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the level of the General Staff this was requested. Requests were made for the state to take measures to prevent such activities, and this was put forward at the Federal Commission. The problems were raised there. Something should have been done on the political level to prevent such things, but I cannot confirm whether anything was actually done at the highest level or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness be shown Exhibit P941, the collegium of the 25th of February, 1999, and I think you will find some of the answers to your questions there. In the English text it's on page 7, paragraph 3, what General Dimitrijevic said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would love to see evidence of what was actually done. I mean, you can talk forever about these things, Mr. Visnjic, but if something was done about them it would help us to know what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we go through this part I think we'll come to the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you should now have before you General Dimitrijevic's remarks, the page in Serbian is 6, it's the last paragraph, and page 7, first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Page 6, this is page 7. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph on page 6 says: "It's to be expected that until the talks are continued the activity of all international institutions in Kosovo and Metohija will continue ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we now turn to page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: " ... We put this on the verification mission of the OSCE with regard to its behaviour up to this point, and we expect that they will monitor all the activities of the security forces; and they will try to collect evidence on their alleged use for purposes other than those that are supposed to be used, the excessive use of force and so on, which should be used for additional pressure on the FRY. It should not be excluded that part of the intelligence gathered will be given -- will be passed on to the terrorist forces." General, does this reflect what General Dimitrijevic told you at the collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this gives a full response to the question of what was presented at the collegium and what the situation was. This makes clear what the situation was and what was expected in the forthcoming period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same document, P941, English text page 9, last paragraph, and page 10, paragraphs 1 and 2. Page 9 in B/C/S, paragraphs 5, 6, and 7. At this part I wish to draw the Court's attention to the third paragraph from the bottom in the English text where General Dimitrijevic says that he proposes that through the federal liaison commission with the OSCE verification mission be cautioned through the federal liaison commission that they should adhere exclusively to their mandate in the agreement signed and that we advise them on our part that we shall no longer tolerate their conduct which goes beyond the mandate given them. And the next paragraph again, the very end of the paragraph where General Dimitrijevic says: "I think that the state commission is best-placed to give them an official warning that this kind of conduct will no longer be tolerated."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did you convey these positions of the General Staff to the Federal Commission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My positions which were prepared for presentation to the Federal Commission were identical to conclusions from the collegium and the chief of the security administration discussed this and this was one of the main tasks and conclusions which had to be presented to the highest state organs, and this was done. And request was made that in this period this should be done as operationally as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's just one more example I would like to give. The collegium of the 11th of March, 1999, Exhibit P935. English page 9 paragraphs 2, 3, 4, and 5, and this again refers to General Dimitrijevic's remarks, the Prosecution often referred to him in the course of their case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The text in Serbian is on page 8, paragraphs 2, 3, 4, and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Dimitrijevic comments on General Krga's remarks about the external factor. And he says the following: "At the same time while external pressure is being exerted they're trying to prevent the activities in the territory of KM aimed at suppressing terrorism primarily through the role performed by the verifying mission which in addition to the intelligence related and subversive activity observed so far is trying to present the terrorist forces, the illegal armed forces of the Kosovo Albanians, and to impose itself as an influence over the international mediator between the parties to the conflict." General, I assume that this is a repetition of what we heard at the previous collegium?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "There are increasingly vocal -- they have investigated whether in Djeneral Jankovic there is one or several barracks, whether the army controls the border crossing in that place, what kinds of weapons the army units securing the Yugoslav-Macedonian have what identifying information there is about the commanders of particular combat groups, whether the army units include Muslim soldiers, what are defence activities are throughout the territory, whether certain units are being demobilised, how the population were to react in the event of an aggression by NATO, whether volunteers are being recruited," and so on. General, in this list is there anything at all falling outside the scope of the Kosovo Verification Mission's task?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conclusion put forward by the chief of the security administration speaks of what was already happening and what was being prepared at that time. One can conclude quite a lot from this as to what was to follow. It's interesting to note that they investigated especially the Djeneral Jankovic area which is close to the Macedonian border so that either the verifiers or somebody else, some other forces, were foreseeing certain activities there. They wanted to have full information about certain areas for the activities which might follow in the coming period. The total assessments carried out in the General Staff - and I'm sure the same assessments were made at a level of the command of the 3rd Corps of the Pristina Corps - that the mission was overstepping the boundaries of the tasks it was set by the agreement and that they were engaging in intelligence work and other work that was not part of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. This concludes the verification mission material. Now I would like to go back a little bit to the planning function of the organ you were in, the operations staff sector. Yesterday you explained the plans being made at a level of the General Staff while you were the chief of this sector, and you said that the plan drawn up in 1999 was the Grom 3 or the Thunderbolt 3 plan. This plan was developed in the second half of January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: However, something happened before this plan was created. On the 15th of January there was an incident in the village of Racak and there was quite a lot of publicity about this. Before we move on to the planning function, let's look at the collegia where the events in Racak were discussed, P939, the collegium, I hope, of the 21st of January, 1999, pages -- in English page 30, the last paragraph and the B/C/S text page 27, last paragraph. General, you will remember that Racak was discussed at the collegium?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'll now show you the remarks of General Ojdanic in connection with this event. Please, explain to us certain points relating directly to some of the participants in the meeting and the organisation of work of the General Staff. General Ojdanic in this last passage on page 30 of the English text says that a Working Group is being set up with General Marjanovic in charge. What was the task of this Working Group?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of the General Staff ordered General Marjanovic, who was his deputy at the time, to set up a Working Group to take the required number of men to assist him to get an overview of the entire situation concerning Racak, study in detail the reports from the subordinate commands and the teams for relations with the missions, to gather information available to various diplomatic institutions and other information, and to prepare an analysis of the actual situation, what really happened around the village of Racak on the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When General Ojdanic says in this sentence: "I'm really embarrassed that I, the Chief of General Staff, have to look someone in the eye and say it is not true." He, in fact, wants to find out what really happened so that he can give arguments when speaking to diplomatic representatives and so that he can explain to them whether the army participated in these events or not.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance attached to the information we had available is shown by the fact that he designated his deputy to be in charge of this group. Secondly, he attempted, not just he but the overall policy of the General Staff was that we should have relevant information, that we should have the truth regardless of what the truth was like. And so he insisted on this and he said that he was embarrassed, it was embarrassing for him as an individual and for the institution as a whole not to know what was going on, especially when dealing with other organs and other countries, representatives of other countries. It was embarrassing for them to have information that he knew nothing about so that he wanted the truth to be discovered at any cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please turn the page. Let's turn the page on both versions, the Serbian and the English. Paragraph 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Ojdanic says: "So whether we participated or not, it doesn't make any sense. I really don't want to be put into that position. In addition to this task, it is the task of this group to see, to explain, the reporting system because this is now our main task, both of the General Staff and of the army, primarily of course the Pristina Corps." What is this in reference to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of the General Staff, among other things, ordered at the time in relation to the previous period to receive daily reports from the command of the Pristina Corps as well in addition to the reports that we were receiving from the 3rd Army. He ordered that the General Staff should now be submitted a daily report by the command of the Pristina Corps in order to make sure there were no discrepancies between the two reports, because normally the corps command would submit reports to the command of the army and the army command to the operations centre of the General Staff. That's why he made this effort to get information from where this was all happening, from the command level, and this was relevant information that we could then use to get at the truth about what was happening. He also ordered, and this was complied with, that additional information be sought, additional reports, on everything that the command of the Pristina Corps knew about the army's activities throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So what happened next, General? Was anything done, were any steps taken, or were these just empty words?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received from the command of the 3rd Army this additional report, the additional report could be used to infer in every way that the army had not been involved in the activities around the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please now show the witness Defence Exhibit 3D559. This is the 28th of January, 1999, collegium. The English reference is page 21, paragraph 1; the B/C/S page 18, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, this is the collegium of the 28th of January, the preceding collegium was held on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were held on a weekly basis, collegium meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Here you have a brief verbal report from General Ojdanic. First let me ask you something else. At the end of this sentence, or rather, this paragraph, there is a reference to the village of Dac. Is there a village called Dac in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What does this paragraph pertain to then?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It pertains to the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In this information you say to General Ojdanic: "General, last time, I was given a task to inform you about the report that we received from the 3rd Army related to the engagement of the army in ..." And then probably inaudible. And then finally: "The official position of the army command, that is, the Army of Yugoslavia, that is the units of the Pristina Corps, did not take part in the action near the village of," now we know it's Racak. General, is this the conclusion that you reached on the basis of that order that General Ojdanic had issued to you with the previous collegium, that is to say to set up a work group to review the documentation and reports, and finally to reach an official conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the final position that I presented at the collegium, and I informed to -- I informed the Chief of General Staff in accordance with his order. Since the operations centre was linked to the first administration and the first administration was in the sector that I was in charge of. Although reports that were arriving those days were set in a detail from both commands, and we came to this conclusion and officially the command of the 3rd Army informed the General Staff that the army, or rather, the units of the Pristina Corps did not take part in the action regarding the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that the Working Group's inquiry was confined to looking at the official reports which had been prepared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that General Marjanovic, as leader of the group, had the task not only to receive the official reports that we were receiving but also other information that he could have received because he often had contacts through the administration for cooperation with international representatives, or rather, the members of the diplomatic corps then in Belgrade, then various press releases that came out then. And he had other information available. On the basis of all those conclusions, this conclusion was reached, that the units did not take part in the actions around the village of Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me this: Did he inquire of members of the KVM what they had discovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received a report from the team in the third command army. And what I said a few moments ago was stated in that, namely, that units of the corps did not take part in the actions regarding the village of Racak. I've already said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now answer my question, please. Did the Working Group get or make any inquiry directly of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since General Marjanovic headed that group, as deputy I cannot confirm whether he had any direct contacts with the verification mission, he personally or any of the members of his Working Group. Often he had contacts with diplomatic representatives who were accredited in our country then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the Working Group make inquiries of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, he had contacts with the representatives of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How was that done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not on his Working Group. The deputy Chief of General Staff headed that, so I cannot confirm for you what organs took part in compiling all this relevant information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you can't really tell us the width of this inquiry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that what was necessary was done, what was indispensable in order to reach important information was done. That is why our General Staff entrusted the deputy chief with leading that team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You must have a basis for that. Was inquiry made of the residents of Racak who survived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm that information for you, whether someone went to the site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have a very long list of people with whom inquiries could have been made, but you really do not know the extent of the inquiry of the Working Group; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The deputy Chief of General Staff headed that team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let us look at Thunder 3, 3D690. Can you tell us under what conditions, or rather, what was the idea, why was this directive made, what was its purpose, and who took part in its drafting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the assessments made in the General Staff in the month of March, or rather, in the beginning of 1999, the overall situation was becoming increasingly complex, especially in the immediate vicinity of our country. The essence of Thunder 3, or rather, the directive for the use of the army was to oppose the violent deployment of a multi-force group that would be stationed in Macedonia and that could be used in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. The essence of this plan is, in addition to these compulsory tasks in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija itself, to take timely measures and elaborate plans and carry out indispensable preparations in order to render impossible the bringing in of this brigade to Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in the directive there is a scenario, I believe, as to what could happen in order for this directive to be used, in fact. Can you tell us something about that without looking at the document; the document will be analysed later on.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The scenario was that in the area of Kosovo and Metohija the terrorist activities would be intensified and that the forces of the army would be scattered in several directions. In order to use this unit that would take part of and -- of Kosovo and Metohija and important facilities therein, and in a way in conjunction with terrorist activities they would make the army unable to resist that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you keep saying "this unit," you're referring to the NATO brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this multi-national brigade that was basically stationed in the territory of the Republic of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to 3D685. Before it appears, tell me who took part in the elaboration of the directive?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The methodology of work in the General Staff was that the General Staff works as a team. The proponent was the sector for operations and staff activities and in it all sectors participated. They gave their contributions from their own lines of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, you mentioned that the Army of Yugoslavia was making certain assessments in terms of intelligence and security and then certain conclusions were based on that and certain scenarios were elaborated for certain plans. I would like to ask you to tell us something about this assessment of the intelligence and security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we please look at page 2 of the English version and of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, you signed this letter that was sent to the Chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed it as one of his assistant chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And you explained there who worked on this assessment and you actually handed in the draft assessment to the Chief of General Staff for him to sign. Do you know whether the Chief of General Staff approved this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that it was a team that worked on this assessment because this was a comprehensive analysis in that period of time, where indeed it was necessary to proceed from the factual situation as it was so that at General Staff level one would see all the important characteristics of the situation that we were in and to have measures taken on the basis of that and, accordingly, to inform the top government echelons as to what the situation was and what should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, later on we will explain this document in greater detail through other witnesses. I just wanted the general to tell me now whether he knows about this document in terms of whether it was presented later to some state authorities, to who, and possibly when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with this document and the overall analysis carried out, the Chief of General Staff prepared and reported to the then-Supreme Defence Council about this, rather, the important conclusions from this assessment made by the General Staff, or rather, the most important conclusions from this assessment that was made by the team that I headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness to comment on document 3D704.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, can you tell me what this document represents, the one that is in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document that was prepared by the Chief of General Staff for reporting to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In it one can see roughly what the plans elaborated were in relation to the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, what was done at General Staff level, what measures should be taken at the level of the state, and he acquainted him with the plans elaborated to date. Here you see plans Thunder 1, Thunder 2, Thunder 3. I talked about that yesterday, there were two stages, the first one being Thunder 1 and the other one is Thunder 2. So that is one plan and two stages. And then there is Thunder 3 that we talked about a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in elaborating this aide-memoire?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the proponent of planning in the General Staff was the sector for operations and staff activities; I said that yesterday. And I and the head of the first administration took part in this in addition to the other members of the General Staff who worked on the elaboration of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, do you know whether after this and up until the beginning of the war there was some other plan at the level of the General Staff that would be related to the situation in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, did any of these plans envisage the relocation or expulsion of the Albanian population from Kosovo or was any military option considered of supporting and assisting such a plan?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, I have never heard of any such plans that you refer to just now, nor did any such plans exist in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at the end of March, or rather, immediately after the outbreak of the war you were assigned another duty, you were appointed commander of the 2nd Army. That is where you replaced General Martinovic; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the end of March I was appointed commander of the 2nd Army in Podgorica instead of General Martinovic who was commander of the 2nd Army until then, and he was assigned to the Ministry of Defence of the Army of Yugoslavia then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, did the dismissal of General Martinovic have anything to do with the dismissal of General Perisic several months before that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see on the basis of what indicators one could link the two. My conclusion is that this has nothing to do with the previous replacement of General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can the witness please now look at P1905.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is a rather lengthy report of the army; you signed it. This is about the resubordination of organs of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro. First of all, can you tell the Trial Chamber whether the area of responsibility of the 2nd Army includes some of Montenegro's territory as well as some of Serbia's territory?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2nd Army, unlike the areas of responsibility of the 1st and 3rd respectively, had a peculiar area of responsibility which included parts of the Republic of Montenegro, most of it, in fact, with the exception of five municipalities that belonged to the navy area, the coastal municipalities. It was also covered by the Podgorica Corps as an operative set-up, and it also included parts of Serbia's west, a total of 21 municipalities, and this was covered by the Uzice Corps. These were two operative set-ups that were part of the 2nd Army of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So, General, by virtue of your position you were in contact with two ministries at the republic level, the MUP of Serbian on the one hand and that of Montenegro. Am I right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My area of responsibility comprised parts of both of these republics, and I wasn't in touch just with these ministries but rather with all the institutions that worked in the area, the local authorities, and everything else that had to do with the life and work of our units as entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You were the person who produced this report, therefore can you briefly explain what sort of problems you encountered while implementing the orders of the Chief of the General Staff on resubordination, specifically the resubordination of Serbia's MUP since this is not about Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to an order of the Supreme Command Staff, the command drafted an order that had to do with the implementation of this task, defining what needed to be done at the level of the army, what needed to be linked to the corps levels in both republics and then further down the chain of command, the border battalions, and that sort of thing and so on and so forth. Based on this order that was addressed to the Ministries of the Interior of both these republics, I received a reply from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Montenegro about this order, whereas the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia did not submit a reply about this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, would I be right if I said that throughout the war Serbia's MUP was never resubordinated to the command of the 2nd Army or to any of its units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serbia's MUP wasn't nor was Montenegro's MUP. These were never resubordinated to the units of the 2nd Army that covered the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Do you know why? Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of the interior of Montenegro did send an explanation as to what the conditions were that were not met for this task to be implemented. I received no explanation nor reply from the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia. In my view, the reason might have been the fact that the official request or order had not gone through the official channels of ministries from the upper-most state level and then down the chain to the Ministry of the Interior for that task to be carried out. I think that may have been the fundamental reason for this failure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, this means that the resubordination order was not submitted down the chain of command all the way down to the Ministry of the Interior, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in the area covered by the 2nd Army, your army, there lived some Albanians, at the same time in the area covered by your army throughout the war there were a large number of Albanians who had fled Kosovo. What about the VJ, the units of your 2nd Army, did you take any measures vis-a-vis these people in terms of driving them across the state border and into Albania? For example, did the VJ take any measures at all vis-a-vis the Albanians who lived in your area, any measures at all that might be defined as expulsion or deportation across the state border?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had been commander of the 2nd Army for eight years by this time, I had been corps commander, and I had been chief of the army staff. I was familiar with Montenegro. There were then, as now, about 7 per cent of Albanians in Montenegro, in Montenegro's ethnic make-up. Never up to that point or at the time, for that matter, were there any problems in the relationship between the army and the local Albanians or anyone else for that matter. There was sporadic border incidents, mostly caused from the Albanian side during my time as corps commander and examination-in-chief of the army staff, but those were dealt with. However, what you asked me about, this never happened in any shape or form during my time there or as far as I know before or after.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You were the army commander. What were the powers of an army commander in terms of using the forces, vis-a-vis the General Staff I mean? What was the commander's discretionary power? What was his authority? What in actual fact could he have done?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was all based on the principle of subordination in the army. So we carried out all of our assignments pursuant to orders received from a superior command. In this case, the army command was subordinated directly to the Chief of the General Staff. These tasks were quite general, the tasks set at that level, which the army command assessed and analysed at its own level and then the army would make decisions to implement those. This is a strategic command with comprehensive tasks. Of course an army command can within his decisions deal with certain problems that he believes must be dealt with within his area. This is precisely what happened. There were tasks of both operative and tactical character, and these were carried out and these had to do with orders that were received from our superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. My last question: Do you know or did you perhaps hear that General Ojdanic was personally involved in some sort of an enterprise or a plan or even abetted it to forcibly expel the Albanian population from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have known General Ojdanic for a long time. We were colleagues in the 2nd Army for a while. I was the commander of the Podgorica Corps and he was the commander of the Uzice Corps. As commanders, as officers, we knew each other quite well. What Mr. Visnjic has just suggested, I have no idea how that could possibly be attributed to him or how the term could be used in relation to General Ojdanic as a human being or an officer, especially someone who was part of our General Staff. Therefore, my categoric reply to that is a resounding no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that concludes my examination. I apologise for any mistakes with numbers, exhibits, and so on and so forth. I believe that we'll have a chance to make things right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Obradovic, the timing is good. It's lunchtime now. We need to break for one hour, so you should be back at quarter to 2.00. Please now leave the courtroom with the usher again, and we shall resume at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, you wish to raise something?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, very briefly, just a procedural matter. My understanding of the orders of the Court for these proceedings is that when the witness comes into court to be cross-examined then the parties who may cross-examine him may -- should notify the other parties as to the documents to be used. This consistently is not being done by the Defence, it's after being notified -- notices are coming at various times, which now causing some amount of inconvenience having regard to the amount of documents. So I take the opportunity through the Court to ask that the order be complied with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you mean that when the witness comes into court to be examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To be examined. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can't remember offhand whether the order specifically related to sharing notifications among cross-examining parties, but it clearly it should have done and the spirit of it clearly intends that to be the case. So could Defence counsel please in future intimate to everyone involved in the case a list of the documents likely to be relied upon as soon as the witness for the Defence has started to give evidence. Now, Mr. Fila, you have some cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour, and also I would like to respond to the Prosecutor. He would do well to -- he would have done well to stick by his own advice when I -- when he had his own case, they had additional documents in addition to each and every witness, and that was the witness took an oath already and I never complained. I think what one's first concern should be to clean up and home then think about elsewhere or make suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure that's entirely right, Mr. Fila, but I hope it doesn't indicate a little retaliation going on. You will now be cross-examined, Mr. Obradovic, starting with Mr. Fila for Mr. Sainovic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Obradovic, I only have a few questions for you. You responded to my colleague, Mr. Visnjic, by saying that you were a member of the state commission for cooperation with the OSCE. This commission was headed by Nikola Sainovic and it was set up by the Government of Yugoslavia. You said that you held meetings once a week. I want to know if these meetings took place in Belgrade or somewhere else, sir, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I was not a member of the state commission. I was there on behalf of the Chief of the General Staff, who was a member of the state commission. I attended meetings of the Federal Commission, and these were normally held on Tuesdays at the SIV building in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: When you attended these meetings, how did they strike you? Did these meetings appear to have a command function or were they of a different nature altogether?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many ministers normally attending these meetings from the federal government and the republican government. This was a matter of analysis, discussion, these were working meetings or at least that was my understanding. People offered their opinions, they talked about certain problems from their own areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Fine. The honourable Judge asked you at one point in time when he talked about the withdrawal of the army based on the Jovanovic agreement, did the verifiers have any means of checking whether we were doing that or did they have to do that by breaking into barracks and counting soldiers and their weapons? General Naumann testified before this Trial Chamber, and the page is 8356, the reference of the transcript. General Naumann confirmed that the Yugoslav side was in full compliance with the terms of the agreement and had indeed withdrawn from Kosovo. Can you tell me how this was established, the fact that we were in compliance with the terms?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the agreement, we forwarded all relevant information to whichever institutions requested such information, and one of these was the mission in its entirety. There were no problems about that, and this was done in relation to each unit individually, its numerical strength, for example. Therefore, one had all the information available to them, the numerical strength of each and every unit, their weapons, equipment, and so on and so forth. Therefore, there was no need for anyone to go to any of the barracks in order to obtain additional [as interpreted]; they had everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were they physically near these barracks, could they possibly have seen you send in a company or a division or a battalion or whatever in very rough terms?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mission in Kosovo - and there weren't that many of them - they grew over time and they had a small office, were directly in touch with the units and with the offices, including the liaison offices. They could always go there and see for themselves. There were some situations where they counted us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You once sent in a fresh contingent of 3.500 soldiers. Did they actually see that happen? Were they there to check?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the bodies were concerned that took those people to Kosovo, they said that there were many people from the mission there when the soldiers got there, those who first arrived and those who were about to leave, both. This was something like a rotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Therefore, there was no need for them to take anything at face value, they sometimes counted and they had all relevant information available to them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they knew exactly what the situation was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let me remind you of a collegium, this is not in e-court, but the Prosecutor has it. I announced that I would be asking questions about this and this was would probably what caused Mr. Stamp's reaction. The date is the 30th of October, 1998. At this collegium, I wouldn't be show [as interpreted] you this, I'm not going to tender this, I just want to remind you. This is when Perisic comments about Kadijevic and you came from the Federal Commission for cooperation with the OSCE and then he objects about the Jovanovic-Geremek Agreement being not sufficiently specific. And then Perisic says in rough terms that: Who did this? I don't know, but for example, where they go controlling the units in barracks and they want to go everywhere and enter all barracks. There is no control of weapons except for the OSCE. They have the right, but when they said the subregional one and these guys want to do it now, too, and so on and so forth. Do you think this constituted a position by General Perisic to these guys entering barracks, generally speaking, briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that the teams of the subregional group exercising control did this with a great deal of precision and reliability. They did this based on valid documents and everything was done in a very objective manner, and the same thing could be said of the verification mission and in keeping with the agreement that we had with NATO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, you've been asked a question about the position of General Perisic; you do not appear to be addressing that question. Could you do that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. General Perisic opposed this because of the terms of the agreement. He said the mission had no authority to enter barracks or try to seek any additional information about the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At this same collegium meeting I came across something very interesting about you. I'll remind you, and if you could please explain, I don't quite understand. This is about the Podujevo group. They should move and then Perisic tells you how this is going to happen, this was a token of good-will, if you remember. And then he goes on to mention something really note-worthy, I'll remind you and you explain if you can, please. "I told those guys: You go ahead, establish some relationship with the Albanian factor, and they should provide you with guarantees and you should provide us with guarantees." And I don't know whether you have it but Tresan signed it and that when they talked. So the US diplomatic mission with them had to for -- and then he goes on to say "in the area, "and then Obradovic, you have this act written by General Tresan, personal envoy of ARK and then we withdrew that. Can you explain who this Tresan is? We don't know what this is about or who he was.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be frank, I really don't remember right now. General Perisic's position is familiar to me but I don't know who this other person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the position was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic's position was that they were influencing -- they should influence the other side in order to make sure what had been agreed would be put into practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Oh, well, this same, or rather, collegium exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have on our screens the collegium of the General Staff dated the 27th of November, 1998, this is page Exhibit P925, this is page 15 in e-court, in Serbian, and page 17 of the English text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, are you content that that last document isn't tendered, that's the collegium of the 30th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had planned to address that issue at the close of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think generally the collegium minutes should be received, most of them are in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I take it you've seen this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's your position about it being used without it being tendered into the process?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think it should be tendered. I have no objections to it not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have no objection to it not. Well, let's -- if you prefer to address it at the end, we shall. It looks as though it may be an isolated document, but we certainly don't want to adopt a practice of lengthy reference to documents that are not actually exhibits in the case. We're now moving to P925. Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Obradovic, you talk about Loncar, something or other, but that doesn't matter. Something else matters. And then he requested that Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic as the subhead of the commission have some sort of advisor for military matters and then you explain this, this last sentence: "I said that he [indiscernible] over the army but that if he should need something, it should go through the Federal Commission, the General Staff and then the Chief of the General Staff would decide." Can we conclude based on this that the chain of command throughout your time in that post was reserved and then nobody was meddling.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I clearly said so at a meeting of the Federal Commission and then upon my return to the General Staff, I briefed the Chief of the General Staff on this, saying that any request to the army should follow the chain of command and that the Chief of the General Staff and the chain of command were the only bodies who could decide on matters such as these.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can I infer based on that that this was indeed done, that this was the procedure followed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Loncar's position had nothing to do with the army, he was busy elsewhere, in a different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So he had no authority to command the army or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, his authority had nothing to do with the army. He had no powers in military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have P928 brought up again, page 10 in e-court, in Serbian and pages 9 and 10 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You spoke about this, Mr. Visnjic asked you a question about this. This is quite a lengthy document, but there is the question of the Judges and this was discussed at the Ministry of Justice, right, I'm talking about the judges who fled Kosovo and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is simply information being presented about a judicial problem in a part of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Last paragraph you say that Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic yesterday requested that a meeting be scheduled in order that extraordinary meeting with ambassadors of European country so that he might be able to draw their attention to the situation, right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the conclusions of the commission's president, that this should be done at the federal level, that certain institutions should be alerted about this problem that is discussed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That means Mr. Sainovic discussed the problem with European ambassadors and he informed them about this, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he did or not, but the conclusion was that the measures would be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. At this same meeting there was talk of a helicopter. What is this helicopter and why was that discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mission's representatives were adamant that a helicopter should be provided for their needs in Kosovo; however, the General Staff and the army did not have sufficient helicopters at its disposal and this also applied to our medical crew, who also needed helicopters should need arise. Therefore, our position was that nothing like that should be provided, but we had assumed the responsibility of assisting them and helping them along.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you see General Aco Dimitrijevic's contribution. We've been dealing with him from day one of this trial, it just seems that nobody seems to be calling him; I wonder why. He says, above all, or rather, he expresses his concern, his furry, if I may put it that way, that the judges were not there, the prosecutors, the entire state structure fled the area. He's complaining that there's no state reaction and then he says: "Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic yesterday apparently ordered that the judges be brought back." Did you see anything to indicate that that type of information? What does that mean, to order the judges back?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot confirm this. I don't know how General Dimitrijevic got it. He probably got it from some other source. I know that the view was that the issue at debate was the problem of the judges and what General Dimitrijevic said I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is this perhaps just military parlance because you keep talking about orders all the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. In the army we use the command mode, orders, commands, but this is not a proper way to talk about things in the political structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We have yet another question that's rather confusing me. It's the last passage in his intervention. He says: "I propose and I don't really have to propose. I think that the MUP had to ensure a certain situation in the field and to resolve this situation with anti-terrorist operations. If the MUP is not able to do so, then we all know how the problem needs to be solved then we need to declare a state in which the army should deal with the problems and that's the end of the story." What's he talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have what you just read to me, what General Dimitrijevic said, but I think that at that period MUP was the main force that dealt with those problems. That was within his purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: But what is it that the army should, if the MUP is not able to then we all know how problems are dealt with then you should declare a state in which the army should deal with those problems. That's the same collegium that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was contradictory to the line of thought that there was no need to take radical measures, state of emergency, or to engage the army, to deploy the army, the opinion was that this should be dealt with with a normal involvement of MUP and the army. And General Perisic also was thinking along the lines and he made some proposals that measures should be taken to declare a state, a state of emergency of imminent threat of war, but this was not accepted in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At this same collegium of the 24th of December, 1998, General Dimitrijevic speaks again and he says: "So" -- well, there's no need. Perhaps we could hear your comment. With all that General Marjanovic said that needed to be elaborated, I think that the main thing is to ensure that nobody, even if Sainovic or any other Sainovic, to solve the problems by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is yet another statement made by General Dimitrijevic that nobody could deal with this, did somebody do that with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can confirm since I did deal with the use of the army at the General Staff and I also dealt with those issues at the Federal Commission. There were no such requests made by Sainovic or by any other state institutions because it was quite clearly delineated by the law who had what powers and who needed to do what. So I don't think that this intervention is actually appropriate to the time and the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You are a colonel-general --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch what the speaker is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What would you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, your questions are not being picked up completely by the interpreter. Could you slow down and ask that question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, you are a Lieutenant-General, that is your rank. General Ojdanic's rank is higher than yours. If anyone were to say that a civilian, no matter what his position were in the Government of Serbia, issued orders to General Ojdanic, who stood at attention and saluted and died of fear because this man is issuing him orders, could you imagine such a situation for a general, in particular General Ojdanic -- well, and you for that matter? What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think General Ojdanic is a man of vast experience as a soldier. I don't think that there is a single institution that he would act in this matter, Sainovic, or X, Y, any other person, that is really out of the question. I said that I knew Ojdanic as a human being and as a professional. We were associates. He was my superior at a number of times. He is a capable, responsible officer. So I think that any such allegation would be completely superfluous and would not deserve any comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would your position be the same in relation to a direct order given by President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same thing. There were no problems, and I don't think that there should have been any problems of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My question I think is rather different from the one you've answered. We have Milosevic as the supreme commander. Would you expect Ojdanic not to react to an order from Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't quite understand. What kind of order that would not be carried out, an order issued by Milosevic, what kind of an order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any order at all. You've not questioned the question that was just put to you. That -- and let me get it correctly. Could you imagine such a situation for a general, in particular General Ojdanic, to take orders from a civilian? And you said you can't imagine that. Now, the orders weren't specified, and I'm asking you the question in relation to President Milosevic, who held the rank or the position of supreme commander of the army. Are you saying that you can't imagine General Ojdanic ever obeying an instruction given to him by Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is a substantial difference in the position of Mr. Sainovic, that we just described, and President Milosevic. President Milosevic was the president of the federal state and his powers as the head of state were quite different from those of the deputy prime minister. So he had the right to command the army in peace and in wartime, so he had this right to command the army, that was one of his rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I dare say he could ask someone else to relay his command to General Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, President Milosevic, if he issued any orders, he issued them directly to the Chief of General Staff and the Chief of General Staff then issued orders within his purview. He could not be some kind of a mediator in the communication with any other organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, we know that that's in theory how it should happen. I'm asking you if there's any physical reason why Milosevic could not relay orders through another person to officers in the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know any other channel that could be used because legally it had to go through the chain of command, and the chain of command went from the president of the state to the Chief of General Staff and then further down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
